topics.title: Nomenclature and structure of the carbonyl group

learn.hook: The vanilla in kulfi, the cinnamon in garam masala and the sharp smell of camphor (kapur) all come from aldehydes and ketones. They share one star: the C=O group.
points: Aldehydes have –CHO (carbonyl bonded to at least one H); ketones have C=O bonded to two carbon groups.

IUPAC: aldehydes end in -al, ketones in -one. HCHO methanal (formaldehyde), CH₃CHO ethanal (acetaldehyde), (CH₃)₂CHCHO 2-methylpropanal, CH₃CH=CHCHO but-2-enal, C₆H₅CHO benzenecarbaldehyde (benzaldehyde).
Ketones: CH₃COCH₃ propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₂CH₃ butan-2-one (ethyl methyl ketone), C₆H₅COCH₃ 1-phenylethan-1-one (acetophenone), C₆H₅COC₆H₅ diphenylmethanone (benzophenone).
The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised and forms three σ bonds in one plane at about 120°; its unhybridised p orbital overlaps with oxygen's p orbital to form a π bond.
Oxygen is more electronegative, so the C=O bond is polar: the carbon is electrophilic (Lewis acid site) and the oxygen nucleophilic (Lewis base site). This is shown by the resonance C=O ↔ C⁺–O⁻.

example.q: Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COCH₃.
steps: Longest chain containing C=O: 5 carbons
Number from the end nearer C=O: C=O at C-2, CH₃ at C-4
Name: 4-methylpentan-2-one

learn.reallife: Vanillin (an aldehyde) is the flavour in vanilla ice cream, and cinnamaldehyde gives dalchini (cinnamon) its aroma in Indian cooking.

games.title: Carbonyl structure
items: The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised.
It forms three σ bonds in a plane.
Bond angles around the carbonyl carbon are about 109.5°.
Oxygen pulls electron density away from it.
Oxygen is more electronegative, making it polar.
Resonance places a partial positive charge on carbon.

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
quiz.explain: Four carbons with C=O at C-2 (numbered to give the lowest locant).
steps: Four-carbon chain with C=O, numbered for the lowest locant.
C=O is at C-2: butan-2-one (not butan-3-one).
Answer: Butan-2-one

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of C₆H₅COCH₃?
quiz.explain: Acetophenone is an ethanone with a phenyl group on the carbonyl carbon.
steps: C₆H₅COCH₃ is a two-carbon ketone (ethanone) with phenyl on the carbonyl carbon.
Name: 1-phenylethan-1-one (acetophenone).
Answer: 1-Phenylethan-1-one
quiz.mistake: Treats the ketone as an aldehyde

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCHO?
quiz.explain: The CHO carbon is C-1; a methyl group sits on C-2 of a propanal chain.
steps: The CHO carbon is C-1 of a three-carbon chain (propanal).
A methyl group sits on C-2: 2-methylpropanal.
Answer: 2-Methylpropanal

quiz.q: What is the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon?
quiz.explain: It forms three σ bonds and one π bond, in a trigonal planar arrangement.
steps: The carbonyl carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond.
Three σ bonds in a plane means sp² hybridisation.
Answer: sp²

quiz.q: Which statement about the carbonyl group is correct?
options: The carbon is nucleophilic and the oxygen is electrophilic
Both atoms carry no partial charge
The carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen is nucleophilic
quiz.explain: Polarisation of C=O leaves carbon partially positive and oxygen partially negative.
steps: Oxygen is more electronegative, so C=O is polarised Cδ⁺–Oδ⁻.
The carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen nucleophilic.
Answer: The carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen is nucleophilic

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCHO?
quiz.explain: Number from the CHO carbon (C-1); the double bond starts at C-2.
steps: Number from the CHO carbon (C-1).
The C=C starts at C-2: but-2-enal.
Answer: But-2-enal

quiz.q: What is the approximate bond angle around the carbonyl carbon?
quiz.explain: sp² hybridisation gives a trigonal planar arrangement with angles near 120°.
steps: The sp² carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar.
Bond angles are about 120°.
Answer: 120°

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles. Reason (R): Due to the polarity of the C=O bond, the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The electron-poor carbon attracts electron-rich nucleophiles.
steps: A: nucleophiles attack the carbonyl carbon. True.
R: C=O polarity leaves the carbon partially positive. True.
Electron-poor carbon attracts nucleophiles, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect polarity with reactivity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What makes the carbon of a C=O group a target for nucleophiles?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Oxygen pulls electrons, leaving the sp² carbon partially positive — a perfect target for nucleophiles!
teach.nudge: Which atom is more electronegative, and what charge does that leave on carbon?

revise.summary: Aldehydes have –CHO and ketones C=O between two carbons; IUPAC names end in -al and -one. The carbonyl carbon is sp² and trigonal planar (~120°), with a σ and a π bond to oxygen. The polar C=O makes carbon electrophilic and oxygen nucleophilic.
focus: IUPAC names of aldehydes and ketones
Hybridisation and geometry of the carbonyl group
remember: HCHO methanal; CH₃CHO ethanal; C₆H₅CHO benzaldehyde
traps: Don't number the chain to give C=O a higher locant (butan-3-one is wrong)
Don't call the carbonyl oxygen electrophilic

topics.title: Preparation of aldehydes and ketones: general methods and aldehyde-specific routes

learn.hook: The Rosenmund catalyst is deliberately 'poisoned' with barium sulphate so the reaction stops at the aldehyde. Sometimes chemists want a lazier catalyst!
points: Oxidation of alcohols: 1° alcohols → aldehydes and 2° alcohols → ketones (e.g. with PCC or K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ under controlled conditions). Dehydrogenation of alcohol vapours over heavy-metal catalysts (Ag or Cu) is used industrially.
Ozonolysis of alkenes followed by Zn dust and water gives aldehydes, ketones or both, depending on the alkene's substituents.
Hydration of alkynes: ethyne + H₂O (HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄) gives ethanal; other alkynes give ketones.
Rosenmund reduction: R–COCl + H₂ →(Pd on BaSO₄) R–CHO + HCl. BaSO₄ poisons the palladium so that the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol.

From nitriles: Stephen reaction — R–CN + SnCl₂ + HCl → imine → hydrolysis → R–CHO. Nitriles and esters can also be reduced selectively to aldehydes by DIBAL-H [diisobutylaluminium hydride, AlH(i-Bu)₂] followed by hydrolysis; DIBAL-H leaves C=C bonds untouched.

example.q: How would you convert benzoyl chloride into benzaldehyde?
steps: Use Rosenmund reduction
C₆H₅COCl + H₂ →(Pd–BaSO₄) C₆H₅CHO + HCl
BaSO₄ poisons Pd so the aldehyde is not reduced to benzyl alcohol
example.answer: Rosenmund reduction with H₂ over Pd–BaSO₄

learn.reallife: Indian bulk-drug makers use DIBAL-H in flavour and drug synthesis because it can stop at the aldehyde stage without disturbing other double bonds in the molecule.

quiz.q: What is the role of BaSO₄ in the Rosenmund reduction?
options: It poisons the Pd catalyst so the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol
It increases the activity of Pd
quiz.explain: A partially deactivated catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage.
steps: Rosenmund: R–COCl + H₂ over Pd on BaSO₄ gives R–CHO.
BaSO₄ poisons Pd so the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol.
Answer: It poisons the Pd catalyst so the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol
quiz.mistake: Thinks BaSO₄ speeds up the reaction

quiz.q: What is the product of the Stephen reaction of CH₃CN?
quiz.explain: SnCl₂/HCl reduces the nitrile to an imine, which hydrolyses to the aldehyde.
steps: Stephen reaction: R–CN + SnCl₂/HCl → imine → hydrolysis → R–CHO.
CH₃CN gives CH₃CHO, ethanal.
Answer: Ethanal
quiz.mistake: Thinks the nitrile is reduced to an amine

quiz.q: Which reagent converts CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₂CN into CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₂CHO without affecting the C=C bond?
quiz.explain: DIBAL-H selectively reduces nitriles (and esters) to aldehydes and leaves C=C alone.
steps: DIBAL-H reduces nitriles to aldehydes after hydrolysis.
It does not affect C=C bonds, unlike H₂/Ni or LiAlH₄ conditions.
Answer: DIBAL-H followed by hydrolysis
quiz.mistake: Picks a reagent that also reduces C=C or the aldehyde

quiz.q: What is formed when ethyne is hydrated with HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄?
quiz.explain: The enol formed first tautomerises to ethanal.
steps: Ethyne + H₂O (HgSO₄, dil. H₂SO₄) forms an enol.
The enol tautomerises to ethanal.
Answer: Ethanal
quiz.mistake: Thinks hydration of an alkyne gives an alcohol

quiz.q: What is obtained when propyne is hydrated in the presence of HgSO₄/H₂SO₄?
quiz.explain: Alkynes other than ethyne give ketones (Markovnikov hydration).
steps: Alkynes other than ethyne give ketones on hydration (Markovnikov).
Propyne gives propanone.
Answer: Propanone

quiz.q: Which method converts a secondary alcohol into a ketone?
quiz.explain: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.
steps: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.
Oxidants such as CrO₃ or PCC are used.
Answer: Oxidation (e.g. with CrO₃ or PCC)

quiz.q: What does ozonolysis of but-2-ene (followed by Zn/H₂O) give?
quiz.explain: The C=C splits in the middle, each half becoming CH₃CHO.
steps: Ozonolysis splits but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, at the C=C bond.
Each half becomes CH₃CHO: two molecules of ethanal.
Answer: Two molecules of ethanal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Esters can be converted into aldehydes using DIBAL-H. Reason (R): DIBAL-H is a strong reducing agent that always reduces esters completely to alcohols.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: DIBAL-H at controlled conditions stops at the aldehyde; R is false.
steps: A: esters can be converted to aldehydes with DIBAL-H. True.
R: DIBAL-H always reduces esters fully to alcohols. False: it can stop at the aldehyde.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks every hydride reagent goes all the way to the alcohol

teach.ask: Gappu has an acid chloride: 'How can I turn it into an aldehyde without making an alcohol by accident?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Rosenmund reduction with H₂ over BaSO₄-poisoned Pd stops at the aldehyde. Clever!
teach.nudge: Which reduction, and why is the catalyst poisoned?

revise.summary: Aldehydes and ketones are made by oxidising or dehydrogenating alcohols, ozonolysis of alkenes and hydration of alkynes (ethyne → ethanal). Aldehydes also come from Rosenmund reduction of acyl chlorides (Pd–BaSO₄), the Stephen reaction of nitriles and DIBAL-H reduction of nitriles and esters.
focus: General methods for aldehydes and ketones
Rosenmund reduction and the role of BaSO₄
remember: Ethyne + H₂O (HgSO₄/H₂SO₄) → ethanal; other alkynes → ketones
traps: Don't say BaSO₄ increases Pd activity
Don't say propyne hydration gives propanal

topics.title: Aromatic aldehydes from hydrocarbons; preparation of ketones

learn.hook: Bitter-almond aroma in sweets and badam-flavoured drinks often comes from benzaldehyde made from toluene. Chemists have several neat ways to stop the oxidation right at the aldehyde.
points: Etard reaction: toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂ forms a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.

Toluene + CrO₃ in acetic anhydride gives benzylidene diacetate, which is hydrolysed by aqueous acid to benzaldehyde. Side-chain chlorination of toluene (Cl₂, light) gives benzal chloride (C₆H₅CHCl₂), which on hydrolysis at 373 K gives benzaldehyde (a commercial method).
Gatterman–Koch reaction: benzene (or a derivative) + CO + HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl gives benzaldehyde.
Ketones from acyl chlorides: 2R–MgX + CdCl₂ → R₂Cd + 2Mg(X)Cl; then 2R′–COCl + R₂Cd → 2R′–CO–R + CdCl₂.
Ketones from nitriles: R–CN + R′MgX, then hydrolysis → R–CO–R′ (e.g. CH₃CH₂CN + C₆H₅MgBr → propiophenone, C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃). Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene + R–COCl (anhydrous AlCl₃) → C₆H₅COR.

example.q: How can acetophenone be prepared from benzene?
steps: Use Friedel–Crafts acylation
C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl →(anhydrous AlCl₃) C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl
example.answer: Benzene + ethanoyl chloride with anhydrous AlCl₃

learn.reallife: Benzaldehyde is used in Indian food and fragrance industries to give an almond-like flavour to sweets and syrups.

quiz.q: What is the Etard reaction?
options: Reduction of benzoyl chloride to benzaldehyde
Formylation of benzene with CO and HCl
Oxidation of toluene by chromyl chloride to benzaldehyde
Oxidation of toluene by KMnO₄ to benzoic acid
quiz.explain: CrO₂Cl₂ forms a complex with toluene which is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde.
steps: Etard reaction: toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂.
The chromium complex is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde.
Answer: Oxidation of toluene by chromyl chloride to benzaldehyde
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Rosenmund or Gatterman–Koch

quiz.q: Which reagents are used in the Gatterman–Koch reaction?
options: CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl
quiz.explain: These reagents introduce a –CHO group into benzene.
steps: Gatterman–Koch reaction introduces –CHO into benzene.
Reagents: CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl.
Answer: CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl

quiz.q: What is the product of CH₃COCl with (CH₃)₂Cd?
quiz.explain: The methyl group from dimethylcadmium replaces Cl, giving CH₃COCH₃.
steps: 2R′–COCl + R₂Cd → 2R′–CO–R + CdCl₂.
CH₃COCl + (CH₃)₂Cd gives CH₃COCH₃, propanone.
Answer: Propanone

quiz.q: What is obtained when ethanenitrile (CH₃CN) reacts with CH₃MgBr followed by hydrolysis?
quiz.explain: R–CN + R′MgX gives R–CO–R′ after hydrolysis: CH₃COCH₃.
steps: R–CN + R′MgX, then hydrolysis, gives R–CO–R′.
CH₃CN + CH₃MgBr gives CH₃COCH₃, propanone.
Answer: Propanone
quiz.mistake: Thinks the nitrile is reduced to an aldehyde

quiz.q: Why is dialkylcadmium preferred over a Grignard reagent for making ketones from acyl chlorides?
options: Grignard reagents do not react with acyl chlorides
Dialkylcadmium is less reactive and does not attack the ketone formed
Cadmium acts as a catalyst only
quiz.explain: A Grignard reagent would add further to the ketone to give a tertiary alcohol.
steps: A Grignard reagent would add again to the ketone, giving a 3° alcohol.
Dialkylcadmium is less reactive and stops at the ketone.
Answer: Dialkylcadmium is less reactive and does not attack the ketone formed
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Grignard reagent is unreactive

quiz.q: What is formed when benzal chloride (C₆H₅CHCl₂) is hydrolysed at 373 K?
quiz.explain: Two Cl on the same carbon are replaced, and the gem-diol loses water to give –CHO.
steps: C₆H₅CHCl₂ has two Cl on one carbon.
Hydrolysis gives a gem-diol which loses water to form –CHO: benzaldehyde.
Answer: Benzaldehyde
quiz.mistake: Thinks the product is an alcohol

quiz.q: Which ketone is obtained when benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃?
quiz.explain: Friedel–Crafts acylation introduces CH₃CO– onto the ring.
steps: Friedel–Crafts acylation puts CH₃CO– on the ring.
Benzene + CH₃COCl (AlCl₃) gives C₆H₅COCH₃, acetophenone.
Answer: Acetophenone

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In the oxidation of toluene with CrO₃ in acetic anhydride, the aldehyde is protected as benzylidene diacetate. Reason (R): This prevents further oxidation of benzaldehyde to benzoic acid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Trapping the aldehyde as a diacetate stops over-oxidation; acid hydrolysis then releases benzaldehyde.
steps: A: CrO₃ in acetic anhydride traps the aldehyde as benzylidene diacetate. True.
R: this prevents further oxidation to benzoic acid. True.
Protection explains its use, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the intermediate is useful

teach.ask: Gappu has toluene: 'How do I oxidise toluene to benzaldehyde without going all the way to benzoic acid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Use chromyl chloride (Etard) or CrO₃ in acetic anhydride, which traps the aldehyde before it becomes an acid!
teach.nudge: Which reagents trap the oxidation at the aldehyde stage?

revise.summary: Benzaldehyde is made from toluene by the Etard reaction (CrO₂Cl₂), CrO₃ in acetic anhydride, or via benzal chloride hydrolysis, and from benzene by Gatterman–Koch (CO + HCl, AlCl₃). Ketones come from acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium, nitriles with Grignard reagents, and Friedel–Crafts acylation.
focus: Ketones from acyl chlorides, nitriles and Friedel–Crafts acylation
traps: Don't use a Grignard reagent with acyl chlorides to make ketones
Don't confuse the Etard reaction with KMnO₄ oxidation to benzoic acid

topics.title: Physical properties, nucleophilic addition and relative reactivity

learn.hook: Acetone in nail-polish remover evaporates fast, yet boils higher than butane of similar mass. Its dipoles explain that — and its chemistry too.
points: Methanal is a gas; ethanal is a volatile liquid; other members are liquids or solids. Boiling points are higher than hydrocarbons and ethers of similar mass (dipole–dipole attraction) but lower than alcohols (no H-bonding between molecules). For M ≈ 58–60: n-butane 273 K < methoxyethane 281 K < propanal 322 K < acetone 329 K < propan-1-ol 370 K.

Lower members (methanal, ethanal, propanone) are miscible with water because they form H-bonds with water; solubility falls with longer chains. Lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent smells; larger ones are more fragrant.

Nucleophilic addition: the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon from a direction roughly perpendicular to the plane of the sp² orbitals; carbon changes from sp² to sp³, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which takes up a proton to give the product.
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones: sterically, ketones have two bulky groups hindering attack; electronically, two alkyl groups reduce the positive character of the carbonyl carbon more.
Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal because the benzene ring's resonance reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.

example.q: Arrange ethanal, propanone and methanal in increasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition.
steps: Methanal: two H atoms, least hindered, most electrophilic
Ethanal: one CH₃ group
Propanone: two CH₃ groups — most hindered and least electrophilic

learn.reallife: Acetone is the main solvent in many nail-polish removers sold in India; its mixing with water comes from hydrogen bonding with water molecules.

games.title: Reactivity and mechanism
items: In nucleophilic addition, the carbonyl carbon changes from sp² to sp³.
Ketones are generally more reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles.
Aldehydes are more reactive (less hindrance, more electrophilic carbon).
Methanal is the most reactive carbonyl compound towards nucleophilic addition.
It has no alkyl groups to hinder or donate electrons.
Benzaldehyde is more reactive than propanal towards nucleophiles.
Ring resonance makes its carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.
It accepts hydrogen bonds from water.

quiz.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons of similar mass?
options: Dipole–dipole attractions between polar C=O groups
quiz.explain: The polar carbonyl group gives strong dipole–dipole forces; there is no O–H for H-bonding among themselves.
steps: The C=O group is polar.
Dipole–dipole attractions raise boiling points above those of hydrocarbons.
Answer: Dipole–dipole attractions between polar C=O groups
quiz.mistake: Thinks carbonyl compounds H-bond with each other

quiz.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar mass?
options: They cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other
They form stronger dipole interactions than alcohols
quiz.explain: Alcohols have O–H groups that H-bond between molecules.
steps: Aldehydes and ketones have no O–H group.
They cannot H-bond with each other, so they boil lower than alcohols.
Answer: They cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other

quiz.q: Which is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
quiz.explain: HCHO has no alkyl groups, so it is least hindered and most electrophilic.
steps: Reactivity falls with more alkyl groups (steric and +I effects).
Methanal has none, so it is the most reactive.
Answer: Methanal

quiz.q: Why are ketones less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles?
options: Two alkyl groups hinder attack and reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon
quiz.explain: Both steric and electronic (+I) effects of two alkyl groups lower reactivity.
steps: Two alkyl groups crowd the carbonyl carbon (steric).
They also reduce its positive character (+I), lowering reactivity.
Answer: Two alkyl groups hinder attack and reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon
quiz.mistake: Gives only one effect or the wrong one

quiz.q: Why is benzaldehyde less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition?
options: Resonance with the benzene ring reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
quiz.explain: Delocalisation of electrons from the ring into C=O makes carbon less electrophilic.
steps: The benzene ring donates electrons into C=O by resonance.
This reduces the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity.
Answer: Resonance with the benzene ring reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon

quiz.q: What change in hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon occurs during nucleophilic addition?
quiz.explain: The trigonal planar carbon becomes tetrahedral in the alkoxide intermediate.
steps: The nucleophile adds to the trigonal planar carbon.
It becomes tetrahedral: sp² changes to sp³.
Answer: sp² to sp³

quiz.q: Why are lower aldehydes and ketones such as propanone miscible with water?
options: They form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
quiz.explain: The carbonyl oxygen accepts H-bonds from water.
steps: The carbonyl oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water.
So lower members like propanone are miscible.
Answer: They form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
quiz.mistake: Thinks they cannot interact with water

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Propanal boils at a lower temperature than propan-1-ol. Reason (R): Propan-1-ol molecules are held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: H-bonding in the alcohol is stronger than dipole–dipole attraction in the aldehyde.
steps: A: propanal boils lower than propan-1-ol. True.
R: propan-1-ol molecules are hydrogen bonded. True.
H-bonding is stronger than dipole forces, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect H-bonding with boiling point

teach.ask: Gappu compares: 'Why does ethanal react with nucleophiles faster than acetone?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Acetone's two methyl groups crowd the carbon and reduce its positive charge, so ethanal reacts faster!
teach.nudge: Name the two effects of alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon.

revise.summary: Aldehydes and ketones boil higher than hydrocarbons (dipole–dipole forces) but lower than alcohols (no H-bonding between molecules). In nucleophilic addition the carbonyl carbon goes from sp² to sp³. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones; benzaldehyde less than propanal.
remember: bp (M ≈ 58–60): n-butane < methoxyethane < propanal < acetone < propan-1-ol
Nucleophilic addition: sp² → sp³ alkoxide intermediate
traps: Don't say carbonyl compounds H-bond with each other
Don't say ketones are more reactive than aldehydes

topics.title: Addition of HCN, NaHSO₃, Grignard reagents and alcohols

learn.hook: Chemists sometimes need to 'hide' a ketone while they work on another part of a molecule. Turning it into a ketal with ethylene glycol does the trick.
points: HCN adds to aldehydes and ketones to give cyanohydrins: >C=O + HCN → >C(OH)CN. The reaction is slow with pure HCN but is catalysed by a base, which generates the stronger nucleophile CN⁻. Cyanohydrins are useful synthetic intermediates.

Sodium hydrogensulphite (NaHSO₃) adds to give crystalline hydrogensulphite addition compounds. The equilibrium lies to the right for most aldehydes and to the left for most ketones (steric reasons). The adducts can be decomposed back by dilute acid or alkali, so this is used to separate and purify aldehydes.
Grignard reagents add to give alcohols after hydrolysis (methanal → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3°).

Aldehydes + one equivalent of a monohydric alcohol in dry HCl give hemiacetals (alkoxy alcohols), and then acetals (gem-dialkoxy compounds). Ketones with ethylene glycol in dry HCl give cyclic ketals. Dry HCl protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic.
Acetals and ketals are hydrolysed back to the carbonyl compound by aqueous mineral acid, so they are used to protect carbonyl groups.

example.q: What is the product when ethanal reacts with HCN, and what type of compound is it?
steps: CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon
The alkoxide picks up H⁺
Product: CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile)

learn.reallife: Protecting groups like ketals are routine in India's drug-synthesis labs, letting chemists build complex medicines one step at a time.

games.title: Reagent with a carbonyl compound ↔ product
pairs: One equivalent of ROH, dry HCl
Excess ROH with an aldehyde, dry HCl
Ethylene glycol with a ketone, dry HCl

games.title: Addition reactions
items: Addition of HCN is catalysed by a base.
Base generates CN⁻, a stronger nucleophile.
Most ketones readily form stable hydrogensulphite addition compounds.
For most ketones the equilibrium lies to the left for steric reasons.
Dry HCl protonates the carbonyl oxygen in acetal formation.
This makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.
Acetals are hydrolysed back to aldehydes by aqueous mineral acids.
That is why they are used as protecting groups.
Ketones react with Grignard reagents to give primary alcohols.

quiz.q: What is the product when propanone reacts with HCN?
quiz.explain: CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon and OH forms on the same carbon: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

topics.title: Addition of ammonia derivatives and reduction

learn.hook: An orange-red precipitate in the 2,4-DNP test tells a lab technician 'carbonyl group present' within seconds — a favourite of CBSE practical examiners.
points: Ammonia derivatives (H₂N–Z) add to aldehydes and ketones and then lose water, forming >C=N–Z. The reaction is reversible and catalysed by acid.

Products: hydroxylamine (Z = OH) → oxime; hydrazine (Z = NH₂) → hydrazone; phenylhydrazine → phenylhydrazone; 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) → 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (yellow, orange or red solid, used to identify carbonyl compounds); semicarbazide → semicarbazone.
Reduction to alcohols: NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ or catalytic hydrogenation reduce aldehydes to 1° alcohols and ketones to 2° alcohols.

Reduction to hydrocarbons: Clemmensen reduction (zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl) and Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine, then heating with KOH in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol) convert >C=O into >CH₂.

CH₃COCH₃ + 4[H] →(Zn–Hg, conc. HCl) CH₃CH₂CH₃ + H₂O

topics.title: Oxidation, Tollens' and Fehling's tests, and the haloform reaction

learn.hook: A silver mirror on the inside of a test tube is one of the prettiest results in a chemistry lab — and a sure sign of an aldehyde.
points: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by HNO₃, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇ and even mild oxidising agents. Ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidants at high temperature, with C–C bond cleavage, giving acids with fewer carbon atoms.
Tollens' test: warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollens' reagent) gives a silver mirror: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 2H₂O + 4NH₃.

Fehling's test: Fehling's A (aqueous CuSO₄) and Fehling's B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate, Rochelle salt) are mixed; aliphatic aldehydes give a reddish-brown precipitate of Cu₂O: RCHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O. Aromatic aldehydes do not give this test.

Haloform reaction: compounds with a CH₃CO– group (methyl ketones and ethanal) are oxidised by sodium hypohalite to the sodium salt of an acid with one carbon less, plus haloform (CHX₃). With NaOI a yellow precipitate of iodoform forms (iodoform test). C=C bonds are not affected.
Distinguishing: Tollens'/Fehling's separate aldehydes from ketones; the iodoform test picks out methyl ketones and ethanal (e.g. pentan-2-one vs pentan-3-one, ethanal vs propanal).

example.q: How would you distinguish between pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one?
steps: Pentan-2-one is CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, a methyl ketone
Pentan-3-one is CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, not a methyl ketone
Warm each with I₂ and NaOH: only pentan-2-one gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform
example.answer: Iodoform test: positive for pentan-2-one only

Answer: Iodoform test: only ethanal gives a yellow precipitate

options: They have no H on the carbonyl carbon, and oxidation would need C–C bond cleavage
They are more reactive than aldehydes

steps: Ketones have no H on the carbonyl carbon.

options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

remember: Fehling's: Cu²⁺ → Cu₂O (red-brown); not given by aromatic aldehydes
Iodoform test: CH₃CO– compounds (and ethanal) → yellow CHI₃

topics.title: α-Hydrogen reactions: aldol and Cannizzaro; ring substitution

learn.hook: Two molecules of ethanal can join hands to make a bigger molecule with a C–C bond — the aldol reaction, one of organic chemistry's most powerful tools.
points: Hydrogens on the carbon next to C=O (α-hydrogens) are acidic because the carbonyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and the resulting carbanion (enolate) is resonance stabilised.

Aldol reaction: aldehydes/ketones with at least one α-H, in dilute alkali, give β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) or β-hydroxy ketones (ketols), which lose water on heating to give α,β-unsaturated compounds. 2CH₃CHO →(dil. NaOH) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) →(heat, −H₂O) CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal). 2CH₃COCH₃ →(Ba(OH)₂) 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one → 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one.

Cross aldol condensation between two different compounds that both have α-H gives a mixture of four products. A ketone can be one partner: benzaldehyde + acetophenone (dilute NaOH) gives 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one (benzalacetophenone).

Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes without α-H, heated with concentrated alkali, undergo self oxidation–reduction (disproportionation): 2HCHO + conc. KOH → CH₃OH + HCOOK; 2C₆H₅CHO + conc. NaOH → C₆H₅CH₂OH + C₆H₅COONa.
Electrophilic substitution: the –CHO/–COR group is deactivating and meta-directing; benzaldehyde with conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄ at 273–283 K gives 3-nitrobenzaldehyde.

example.q: Which of these undergo aldol condensation and which undergo Cannizzaro reaction: ethanal, methanal, benzaldehyde, propanone?
steps: Ethanal (CH₃–CHO) has α-H → aldol
Propanone (CH₃COCH₃) has α-H → aldol
Methanal (HCHO) has no α-carbon → Cannizzaro
Benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) has no α-H → Cannizzaro
example.answer: Aldol: ethanal, propanone; Cannizzaro: methanal, benzaldehyde

topics.title: Uses of carbonyl compounds; naming and structure of carboxylic acids

learn.hook: Red ants sting with formic acid, vinegar gets its tang from acetic acid, and rancid butter smells of butyric acid. Many common names come from these natural sources.
points: Uses of carbonyl compounds: formalin (40% aqueous methanal) preserves biological specimens and is used to make bakelite (phenol–formaldehyde resin) and urea–formaldehyde glues; ethanal is a starting material for acetic acid, ethyl acetate, vinyl acetate, polymers and drugs; benzaldehyde is used in perfumery and dyes; acetone and ethyl methyl ketone are common industrial solvents; vanillin, acetophenone and camphor are prized for odour and flavour.

Carboxylic acids (–COOH): HCOOH formic acid (methanoic acid, from Latin formica, ant); CH₃COOH acetic acid (ethanoic acid, from acetum, vinegar); CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH butyric acid (butanoic acid, from butyrum, butter).

More names: HOOC–COOH oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid); HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH adipic acid (hexanedioic acid); C₆H₅COOH benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid); C₆H₄(COOH)₂ phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid).

In the carboxyl group, the bonds to the carbon lie in one plane about 120° apart. The carbonyl carbon is less electrophilic than in aldehydes and ketones because the lone pair on the –OH oxygen is delocalised onto the C=O (resonance).

learn.hook: Need benzoic acid for a food preservative? Start from toluene, from bromobenzene with dry ice, or from benzonitrile. Chemistry offers many roads to the same –COOH.
points: From primary alcohols and aldehydes by oxidation: KMnO₄ (neutral, acidic or alkaline), K₂Cr₂O₇ or CrO₃ in acidic medium (Jones reagent). Aldehydes are oxidised even by mild oxidants.

From nitriles and amides: hydrolysis with H⁺ or OH⁻; nitriles first give amides (under mild conditions the reaction can be stopped there), then acids.
From Grignard reagents: R–MgX + CO₂ (dry ice), then H₃O⁺ → R–COOH, an acid with one more carbon than the alkyl halide.

topics.title: Physical properties and acidity of carboxylic acids

learn.hook: Acetic acid boils at 391 K, way above ethanol, even though their masses are similar. And it fizzes with baking soda, which phenol cannot do.
points: Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of similar mass, because of extensive hydrogen bonding. Many exist as hydrogen-bonded dimers in the vapour phase and in aprotic solvents.

Simple aliphatic acids up to four carbons are miscible with water (H-bonding); solubility falls as the chain grows. Benzoic acid is nearly insoluble in cold water. Acids also dissolve in less polar solvents like benzene, ether and chloroform.

Acids react with metals (giving H₂), with alkalis (salt + water), and with weak bases such as NaHCO₃, giving brisk effervescence of CO₂ — a test that phenols do not pass: R–COOH + NaHCO₃ → R–COONa + H₂O + CO₂.

Acid strength: Ka = [H₃O⁺][RCOO⁻]/[RCOOH], pKa = −log Ka; smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4–5, e.g. CH₃COOH 4.76, C₆H₅COOH 4.19, HCOOH 3.75) are weaker than mineral acids but stronger than phenols (≈10) and alcohols (≈16), because the carboxylate ion has two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge on two electronegative oxygen atoms.

Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity (CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > CH₂ClCOOH > CH₃COOH; FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH), with a smaller effect the farther they are from –COOH. Electron-donating groups (alkyl) decrease acidity; a phenyl or vinyl group directly attached increases it relative to acetic acid.

example.answer: pKa = 5; it is slightly weaker than acetic acid

topics.title: Reactions involving C–OH cleavage and the –COOH group

learn.hook: Fruity smells of esters, the pain-relief paracetamol (an amide) and the nylon in your schoolbag straps all come from reactions where the –OH of an acid is replaced.
points: Anhydride formation: heating with a dehydrating agent such as P₂O₅ or conc. H₂SO₄ gives acid anhydrides: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O.

Esterification: R–COOH + R′–OH ⇌(H⁺) R–COOR′ + H₂O. Mechanism: (1) protonation of the carbonyl oxygen; (2) nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the carbonyl carbon; (3) proton transfer in the tetrahedral intermediate, making –OH₂⁺ a good leaving group; (4) loss of water; (5) loss of H⁺ from the protonated ester.
Acid chlorides: R–COOH + PCl₅ → R–COCl + POCl₃ + HCl; 3R–COOH + PCl₃ → 3R–COCl + H₃PO₃; R–COOH + SOCl₂ → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCl (preferred: gaseous by-products).
Amides: R–COOH + NH₃ ⇌ RCOO⁻NH₄⁺ →(heat) R–CONH₂ + H₂O. Phthalic acid with NH₃ gives phthalamide, and on strong heating, phthalimide.

Reduction: LiAlH₄ or diborane (B₂H₆) reduce –COOH to –CH₂OH (diborane does not easily reduce esters, nitro or halo groups; NaBH₄ does not reduce –COOH). Decarboxylation: sodium carboxylates heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO, 3 : 1) lose CO₂ to give an alkane with one carbon fewer; Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous salts gives an alkane with twice the carbons of the alkyl group.

topics.title: HVZ reaction, ring substitution, uses and multi-step conversions

learn.hook: Board exams love 'Convert A into B in not more than two steps'. Knowing a handful of key reactions — HVZ, Rosenmund, Grignard, oxidation — unlocks most of them.
points: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction: acids with an α-hydrogen, treated with Cl₂ or Br₂ and a small amount of red phosphorus, then water, give α-halo acids: R–CH₂–COOH → R–CH(X)–COOH.

The –COOH group is deactivating and meta-directing: benzoic acid gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) and 3-bromobenzoic acid (Br₂/FeBr₃). Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions because –COOH deactivates the ring and the AlCl₃ catalyst binds to the carboxyl group.

Uses: methanoic acid in rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating industries; ethanoic acid as a solvent and as vinegar; hexanedioic acid for nylon-6,6; esters of benzoic acid in perfumery; sodium benzoate as a food preservative; higher fatty acids for soaps and detergents.

Common conversions: toluene → benzoic acid (KMnO₄); benzoic acid → benzaldehyde (SOCl₂, then Rosenmund); ethanoic acid → 2-chloroethanoic acid (HVZ); ethanol → 3-hydroxybutanal (oxidise to ethanal, then aldol); benzene → m-nitroacetophenone (Friedel–Crafts acylation, then nitration).

steps: Step 1 (HVZ): CH₃COOH + Cl₂ (red P), then H₂O → ClCH₂COOH
Step 2: ClCH₂COOH + aqueous KOH → HOCH₂COOK
Acidify → HOCH₂COOH

teach.ask: Gappu is stuck on a conversion: 'How do I turn ethanoic acid into chloroethanoic acid?'

revise.summary: The HVZ reaction (X₂ + red P, then water) gives α-halo acids from acids with α-H. –COOH is deactivating and meta-directing, and benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts. Uses include vinegar, adipic acid for nylon-6,6 and sodium benzoate as a preservative.
remember: Adipic acid → nylon-6,6; sodium benzoate → food preservative
traps: Don't say benzoic acid undergoes HVZ
